title: Presenting and leading a discussion
cando: give a clear presentation, handle questions and plan your English after the course

about.text: This is the last lesson of the Intensive English course. You give a short talk, handle questions and lead a discussion, and you write a plan for your English for the next six months. At the end, you give a five-minute presentation and take the B2 check.
goals: Guide your audience with signposts: I'd like to start by… Moving on to… To sum up…
Put weight on the key idea: What matters is…, It was… that…
Handle questions, even when you're not sure of the answer.
Read a learning plan, and write a realistic plan for your next six months.
Give a five-minute presentation, lead the discussion, and show your English at B2.

chapters.title: A short talk at work
chapters.text:
This is the last lesson of the course. In it, you give a talk, you lead a discussion, and you plan your English for after the course.
First, you listen to Mei. She leads a customer service team, and her team has just finished a trial of a live chat service. She presents the results at a team meeting.
Listen to how she guides her audience. I'd like to start by giving you an overview. Moving on to the feedback. To sum up.
These phrases are signposts. They tell the listener where they are in the talk.
Then listen to how she answers questions. That's a good question. Off the top of my head, I'd say four, but let me check.

chapters.title: Signposts, and putting weight on an idea
chapters.text:
Now the grammar. There are two points.
First, signposts. You open: I'd like to start by. You move on: Moving on to. You point at a visual aid: As you can see on the chart. And you close: To sum up.
Second, putting weight on an idea. In writing, you can use bold type. In speech, you use grammar.
What matters is the result. The key idea comes at the end, after is.
It was the team that made it work. The key idea comes straight after it was, and your voice stresses it.
Don't use these in every sentence. Save them for the one or two ideas that you want people to remember.

chapters.title: Your plan after the course
chapters.text:
Next, you read Ana's learning plan for the next six months.
Notice three things. She chooses one priority, not five. She names a time and a place, not just an amount: a podcast on the train, not an hour a day. And she says what might go wrong.
Then you write your own plan. Be honest about where you are, and make it realistic. A small plan that you follow is worth more than a big plan that you give up.
Then check your plan with three questions. Is there only one priority? Does it name a time and a place? Would I still do it in a busy week?

chapters.title: Your final presentation
chapters.text:
Then you give a five-minute presentation, and you lead the discussion after it.
Choose a topic you know well: a project at work, a change you'd like to see, or your plan for your English.
Rehearse it out loud, twice, with a timer. Nerves are normal, and a slow first sentence helps.
After the talk, you lead the discussion. Take questions. Ask the group a question of your own. And make sure everybody gets a turn.
Then you take the B2 check, in listening, reading, writing and speaking. Take your time, and show what you can do.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer story or article about speaking in front of others.
Read it once for the main events. Then read it again, and notice how the speaker prepares, and how they deal with the unexpected.
And then, well done. You've reached the end of the course. Keep going.

warmup.prompt: You have to give a short talk at work tomorrow. What helps you most?
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many speakers practise out loud at least twice. It helps with the timing, and it calms the nerves.

conversation.title: A short talk at work
conversation.setting: Mei Chen leads the customer service team at Oakwell Home, an online furniture company. The team has just finished a three-month trial of a live chat service, and Mei presents the results at a team meeting.
lines: Mei
Good morning, everyone, and thanks for coming. I'd like to start by giving you a quick overview of our live chat trial. There'll be time for Q&A at the end.
Mei
First, the results. As you can see on the chart, customers on live chat waited four minutes on average. On the phone, it was eleven.
Mei
Moving on to the feedback. It wasn't the speed that customers liked most. It was being able to send a photo of the problem.
Mei
I'd also like to highlight the team's role. What made this work was your input in the first week, not the software.
Mei
So, to sum up: shorter waits, happier customers, and a service that you helped to design. What matters now is deciding whether we keep it. I'm happy to take any questions.
Kwame
Thanks, Mei. How many people would we need to run the chat all day?
Mei
That's a good question. Off the top of my head, I'd say four, but let me check the figures and send them round this afternoon.
Lena
Can I come in here? Some of us found the chat tricky at busy times, with three conversations open at once.
Mei
That's a fair point, and it's in the handout. We're suggesting a limit of two chats per person.
Kwame
Would we need extra training for that?
Mei
Possibly. Why don't we brainstorm it now, for five minutes? Let's take turns, so everyone gets a say.
Lena
Good idea. I'll start.
Mei
Great. And I'll keep an eye on the time, so that we stay on track.

questions.q: What did customers like most about live chat?
questions.a: being able to send a photo of the problem
questions.why: Mei says: It wasn't the speed that customers liked most. It was being able to send a photo.

questions.q: How many people does Mei think they would need?
questions.a: about four, but she will check
questions.why: Mei says: Off the top of my head, I'd say four, but let me check the figures.

questions.q: What does Mei suggest when Lena says the chat was tricky at busy times?
questions.a: a limit of two chats per person
wrong: closing the chat at busy times
moving busy customers to the phone
questions.why: Mei says: We're suggesting a limit of two chats per person.

items.meaning: The people who watch or listen to a talk, a play or a programme.
items.example: Think about your audience: a talk for managers is different from a talk for new staff.

items.meaning: A short description of the main points, without the details.
items.example: The first slide gives an overview of the whole project.

items.meaning: A sheet of paper with information that you give to people at a talk or a meeting.
items.example: All the figures are on the handout, so you don't need to write them down.

items.meaning: Something the audience can look at, such as a slide, a chart or an object, that helps them understand.
items.example: A simple chart is often the best visual aid.

items.meaning: To practise a talk or a performance before you give it.
items.example: I rehearsed my presentation three times the night before.

items.meaning: The nervous feeling you have before something important.
items.example: Everyone has nerves before a big talk, and a slow first sentence helps.

items.meaning: To get people's attention and keep them interested.
items.example: Asking a question at the start is a good way to engage the audience.

items.meaning: To make something stand out, so that people notice it.
items.example: I'd like to highlight three points from the report.

items.meaning: To share a lot of ideas quickly in a group, before you judge them.
items.example: Let's brainstorm some names for the new service.

items.meaning: Ideas, advice or information that people give to help a piece of work.
items.example: Thanks for your input: it changed the whole plan.

items.meaning: To do something one after another, so that everyone has a chance.
items.example: Let's take turns to give feedback, starting with Omar.

items.meaning: Going as planned, without moving away from the plan or the topic.
items.example: We're on track to finish the project by June.

items.meaning: Questions and answers: the time after a talk when the audience asks questions.
items.example: There'll be ten minutes for Q&A at the end.

items.meaning: Difficult, and needing care.
items.example: That's a tricky question, so let me think about it.

items.w: off the top of my head
items.meaning: Without checking or thinking carefully; from memory.
items.example: Off the top of my head, I'd say about forty customers, but I'll check.

sound.title: Stress on the idea that matters
sound.explain: When you put weight on an idea, your voice does it too. After It was or It wasn't, the strongest stress falls on the key idea: the team, the photos, the price. In What… is…, stress the key word at the end. Listen, then say each group and line.
groups: It was the team · It was the photos · It wasn't the price
What matters is the result · What they liked was the photos
lines: It was the team that made it work.
What matters now is the decision.
It wasn't the speed that customers liked most. It was the photos.

sayIt.instructions: Say Mei's lines as if you were giving the talk. Record yourself, then listen back. Do you slow down, and stress the key idea in each sentence?
lines: Good morning, everyone, and thanks for coming. I'd like to start by giving you a quick overview of our live chat trial.
Moving on to the feedback. It wasn't the speed that customers liked most. It was being able to send a photo of the problem.
So, to sum up: shorter waits, happier customers, and a service that you helped to design. What matters now is deciding whether we keep it.
That's a good question. Off the top of my head, I'd say four, but let me check the figures and send them round this afternoon.

spot.instructions: Look at these sentences from Mei's talk. Some guide the audience through the talk. Others put weight on one idea.
examples: I'd like to start by giving you a quick overview of our live chat trial.
It wasn't the speed that customers liked most. It was being able to send a photo of the problem.
What made this work was your input in the first week, not the software.
What matters now is deciding whether we keep it.
spot.question: Which sentences tell the audience where they are in the talk? Which ones put weight on an idea? Where does the important idea go in each one?
spot.answer: I'd like to start by… and Moving on to… are signposts: they guide the audience. It wasn't… that…, What made this work was… and What matters now is… put weight on an idea. After It was, the key idea comes straight away: being able to send a photo. With What… is/was…, it comes at the end: your input, deciding whether we keep it.

rules.title: Signposting a talk
rule: Start: I'd like to start by + -ing… / I'm going to talk about three things.
Move on: Moving on to… / That brings me to… / Next, let's look at…
Point at a visual aid: As you can see on the chart… / If you look at the handout…
End: To sum up… / I'm happy to take any questions.
Questions: That's a good question. / Can I come back to you on that?
rules.mistake: Not: I'd like to start by give you an overview. Say: I'd like to start by giving you an overview.

rules.title: Putting weight on an idea: What matters is…, It was… that…
rule: What + clause + is/was + the key idea: What matters is the result.
It was + the key idea + that…: It was the team that made it work.
Negative first, then the point: It wasn't the price that worried them. It was the delay.
Your voice stresses the key idea: It was the TEAM that made it work.
Use one or two in a talk, at the key moments, not in every sentence.
rules.mistake: Not: What matters it is the result. Say: What matters is the result.

practice.q: I'd like to start ___ you a quick overview.
That ___ me to my last point: the costs.
practice.why: That brings me to… moves the talk to its next part.

practice.q: ___ on to the second part of the talk: the costs.
practice.why: Moving on to… is the usual signpost for the next part.

practice.q: As you can ___ on the chart, calls fell by half.
practice.why: As you can see… points at a visual aid.

practice.q: What ___ is the result, not the method.
practice.why: What + verb + is: What matters is…

practice.q: It was the late delivery ___ upset the customer.
practice.why: It was + the key idea + that…

practice.q: ___ customers liked most was the photo feature.
practice.why: What… was… puts the key idea at the end.

practice.q: It wasn't the price that worried them. ___ the delay.
practice.why: Negative first, then the real point: It wasn't… It was…

practice.q: To sum ___ , the trial was a success.
practice.why: To sum up starts the summary at the end of a talk.

practice.q: Someone asks a question you can't answer. You say: That's a good question. Can I ___ to you on that?
practice.why: Can I come back to you on that? promises an answer later.

yourTurn.prompt: Think of a project, a change at work or something you have learned. Write the opening and the end of a short talk about it. Use two signposts, one sentence with What… is/was… and one with It was… that…
yourTurn.model: I'd like to start by telling you why we changed the rota. Moving on to the results: sick days fell by a third in six months. What matters most is that people now know their shifts two weeks ahead. It was the night team that suggested it, so thank you. To sum up: a small change, and a big difference.

text.title: Ana's plan for the next six months
text.body:
MY ENGLISH PLAN: THE NEXT SIX MONTHS
Name: Ana Costa
Written: 1 June
Review: 1 December

1. Where I am now
I have just finished Level 4 of the Intensive English course. My reading and writing are strong: I can write a formal letter or a report with few mistakes. I speak fluently one to one, but I still struggle in fast meetings with several native speakers, where people interrupt each other and change the topic without warning.

2. My priority
One priority only: following and joining in fast meetings. Grammar and formal writing can wait until December, although I will keep using them at work.

3. What I will do, and when
• Listening: a twenty-minute business podcast on the train to work, Monday to Friday. With English subtitles for the first month, then without.
• Speaking: on the walk home, twenty minutes saying useful phrases from the podcast out loud. At work, one comment or question in every team meeting, however short.
• At the weekend: one film or episode of a series in English, with English subtitles.
I will set aside forty minutes a day for this plan, and no more. A realistic plan that I follow is better than an ambitious one that I give up.

4. How I will keep going
Consistency matters more than long sessions. If I miss a day, I will not try to catch up with a double session. I will simply start again the next day. Self-discipline is easier with a routine, so I will dedicate the same train journey to the podcast every day.

5. How I will assess my progress
Once a month, I will record myself summing up a meeting in two minutes, and compare it with my first recording. In December, I will ask my manager whether I contribute more in meetings.

6. What might go wrong
August is always busy at work. If I lose a week, I will cut the plan to ten minutes a day rather than stop.

What I hope for: a breakthrough in meetings, when I stop translating in my head and just join in.

gist.q: What is Ana's plan mostly about?
gist.a: getting better at fast meetings with several speakers
wrong: improving her grammar and formal writing
passing a written exam in December
gist.why: Section 2 says: one priority only, following and joining in fast meetings.

gist.q: What kind of plan has Ana made?
gist.a: a small daily plan that she can keep up
wrong: a plan to study for several hours a day
a plan that her manager wrote for her
gist.why: She says a realistic plan that she follows is better than an ambitious one that she gives up.

detail.q: How much time a day will Ana spend on the plan?
detail.why: Section 3: forty minutes a day for this plan, and no more.

detail.q: When will she stop using subtitles with the podcast?
detail.why: Section 3: with English subtitles for the first month, then without.

detail.q: What will she do if she misses a day?
detail.a: start again the next day, without a double session
wrong: do twice as much the next day
stop the plan until the weekend
detail.why: Section 4: I will not try to catch up with a double session.

detail.q: How will she assess her progress every month?
detail.a: by recording a two-minute summary of a meeting and comparing it with her first one
wrong: by asking her manager for a score
detail.why: Section 5: she records herself summing up a meeting, and compares it with her first recording.

items.meaning: The most important thing, which you deal with first.
items.example: My priority this year is speaking up in meetings.

items.meaning: Possible to do in real life, and based on what is really true.
items.example: Twenty minutes a day is a realistic target for a busy parent.

items.meaning: To give your time or effort to one particular purpose.
items.example: I dedicate my Friday lunch break to reading in English.

items.meaning: To keep some time or money for one particular purpose.
items.example: I set aside half an hour every evening for practice.

items.meaning: Doing something regularly, in the same way, over a long time.
items.example: In language learning, consistency matters more than long sessions.

items.meaning: The ability to make yourself do something, even when you don't feel like it.
items.example: It takes self-discipline to study after a long day at work.

items.meaning: A sudden, important improvement after a long time of trying.
items.example: My breakthrough came when I stopped translating everything in my head.

items.meaning: To judge how good something is, or how much progress has been made.
items.example: The final check assesses listening, speaking, reading and writing.

items.meaning: A person who has spoken a language since they were a small child.
items.example: Don't try to sound like a native speaker. Try to be clear.

items.meaning: A recorded programme that you can listen to online, often one of a series.
items.example: I listen to a news podcast on my way to work.

items.meaning: Words on the screen that show what people in a film or a programme are saying.
items.example: Try watching with English subtitles, not subtitles in your own language.

model.title: Omar's six-month plan
model.body:
Where I am: I have just finished Level 4. I read and write well, but I find it tricky to speak on the phone, especially to people I don't know.
My priority: phone calls at work. Everything else can wait until the spring.
What I will do: I will set aside fifteen minutes every lunchtime. Twice a week, I will listen to a podcast about customer service. On the other days, I will practise a call with Wehel, and then make one real call instead of sending an email.
How I will keep going: the same time every day, so that it becomes a habit.
How I will assess it: once a month, I will record a practice call and compare it with the first one.
What might go wrong: December is our busiest month. If I have no time, I will do five minutes, not nothing.
My hoped-for breakthrough: making a call without writing a script first.

write.task: Write your own learning plan for the next six months, in 150 to 200 words. Use the headings in the model. Be honest about where you are, choose one priority, and make the plan realistic: a time, a place and an amount that you can keep.
write.starter: Where I am: I have just finished Level 4. …
checklist: I named one priority, not five.
I said when and where I will practise, not just how much.
I said how I will assess my progress, and when.
I said what might go wrong, and what I will do then.

card.title: Your final presentation
card.situation: This is the last task of the course. Choose a topic that you know well: a project at work, a change you would like to see, a skill you have learned, or your plan for your English. You speak for five minutes, and then you lead a short discussion.
card.goal: Give a clear talk with signposts. Take questions, then lead the discussion so that everyone gets a say. After that, take the B2 check.

phrases: I'm going to talk about three things: …
To sum up, … I'm happy to take any questions.
That's a good question. What do the rest of you think?
prepare.notes: Plan the talk in three parts, with one main message. Write your signposts on a card, not the whole talk. Rehearse it twice, out loud and with a timer. Then prepare two questions for the group, in case nobody speaks first.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, give your five-minute presentation. Then lead the discussion: take questions, ask the group one question of your own, and make sure everyone gets a turn. Your teacher tells you when and how you take the B2 check.
doIt.wehel: You are my audience. I will give a five-minute talk. Listen, then ask me three questions, one at a time, and make one of them tricky. After that, tell me: Was my talk clear? Did I use signposts? Did I answer the questions well? Give me one thing to improve. Use clear English.

model.title: Leading the discussion
lines: You
So, to sum up: one priority, a small daily habit, and a check every month. I'm happy to take any questions.
Samir
Thanks, that was really clear. How did you choose your priority?
You
That's a good question. It was the meetings that cost me most at work, so the choice was easy.
Lena
What if you don't have forty minutes a day?
You
Then I'd do less, but every day. What matters is consistency, not the amount.
Samir
Did you think about a teacher, instead of podcasts?
You
That's a tricky one. Off the top of my head, I'd say a teacher is better for speaking, but it costs more. Lena, what do you think?
Lena
I did both. Podcasts were fine for listening, but I needed a real person to practise speaking with.
You
That's useful input. Let's take turns: what's the one thing that helped you most? Samir, would you like to start?
Samir
Subtitles. I watched everything with English subtitles for a year.
You
Great. We've got two minutes left, so let's stay on track. Lena?
Lena
For me, it was a weekly conversation with a friend. It's easier to keep going when you enjoy it.
You
Thanks, both of you. So: podcasts for listening, a real person for speaking, and subtitles to help. Thank you all for your ideas.
compare: Did your talk have a clear start, middle and end, with signposts?
Did you answer questions honestly, and say so when you weren't sure?
Did you ask the group a question, and give everyone a turn?
Did you sum up the discussion at the end?

canDo: I can give a clear talk with signposts: I'd like to start by…, Moving on to…, To sum up…
I can put weight on the key idea: What matters is…, It was… that…
I can handle questions, even when I'm not sure of the answer.
I can lead a discussion so that everyone gets a say.
I can write a realistic plan for my English after the course.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is speaking to an audience, and how do you think they feel?
reading.talk: What did the speaker in the story do well, and what would you do differently? Then think about yourself: what is the first thing you will do for your English after this course? Write a short paragraph, or talk about it with Wehel.

quiz.q: I'd like to start ___ giving you an overview.
quiz.why: Start by + -ing: I'd like to start by giving…

quiz.q: If you look at the ___ , you'll find all the figures there.
quiz.why: A handout is the sheet of information you give people at a talk.

quiz.q: ___ matters most is the customer's experience.
quiz.why: What + verb + is… puts the key idea at the end.

quiz.q: It was the new manager ___ changed the rota.
quiz.why: It was + the key idea + that…

quiz.q: Someone asks a hard question. You say: That's a ___ question. Let me think.
quiz.why: That's a good question thanks the person and gives you a moment to think.

quiz.q: Give everyone a chance to speak, one after another: Let's take ___ .
quiz.why: Take turns means one after another, so that everyone has a chance.

quiz.q: A plan that you can really keep is a ___ plan.
quiz.why: Realistic means possible to do in real life.

quiz.q: By the time the meeting started, we ___ for an hour.
quiz.why: Had been + -ing: an activity that ran up to a moment in the past.

quiz.q: Sales rose ___ 12% last year, to £2 million.
quiz.why: Rise by gives the size of the change; rise to gives the new level.

quiz.q: A formal letter that starts Dear Ms Okafor ends with ___ .
quiz.why: A letter that starts with a name ends with Yours sincerely.

liveClass: Day 1: practise Mei's talk in pairs, one presenting and one asking questions. Then each learner gives a one-minute talk about their work, with two signposts and one sentence with What matters is… or It was… that…

Day 2: the final presentations. Each learner gives a five-minute talk and leads a short discussion (use groups if the class is large). Give feedback on the signposts, and on how each speaker handled the questions.

Day 3: talk about the book. Then learners share their six-month plans in small groups, and each group helps one person make their plan more realistic. Close the course together, and go through how the B2 check works.
